title: TRACE: Time-Adaptive Residual Attention Control with Content–Style Decomposition for Training-Free Diffusion Style Transfer

paper.title: TRACE: Time-Adaptive Residual Attention Control with Content–Style Decomposition for Training-Free Diffusion Style Transfer
paper.abstract: Abstract Reference-guided style transfer aims to preserve the semantic structure of a content image while transferring the visual appearance of a style reference. Recent diffusion-based methods achieve impressive stylization quality by exploiting strong pretrained generative priors. However, training-free approaches still face a difficult trade-off among style fidelity, content preservation, and content leakage. Direct style injection may unintentionally transfer semantic content from the style image, while fixed guidance schedules often ignore the time- and state-dependent nature of diffusion sampling. To address these limitations, we propose TRACE , a training-free diffusion style transfer framework with T ime-adaptive R esidual A ttention Control and C ontent-Style d E composition. TRACE first performs offline CLIP-based subspace analysis to separate content and style directions from paired data. During inference, it removes content-related components from the style reference and style-related components from the content reference to reduce leakage. It then injects style information through residual cross-attention and applies uncertainty-aware guidance to adapt the guidance signal at each denoising step. Experiments show that TRACE achieves a favorable trade-off between stylization and preservation. Compared with optimal-control-based baselines, TRACE substantially improves style fidelity (+17.28 CSD and +34.10 SRA). While, compared with stylization methods, it better preserves content structure (+12.80 DINO, +5.52 CLIP-I, and -8.19 LPIPS) and reduces directional semantic leakage by 29.5% in DCL. Our code is publicly available at TRACE .

sections.heading: 1 Introduction
sections.text: Image style transfer aims to synthesize an image that preserves the semantic structure of a content image while adopting the visual appearance of a style reference. Early neural style transfer methods demonstrated that deep features can separate and recombine content and style representations [ 10 ] , while arbitrary style transfer methods improved efficiency through feature-statistics matching, whitening-and-coloring transforms, attention matching, and transformer-based fusion [ 17 , 20 , 22 , 8 ] . More recently, diffusion models have provided strong generative priors for high-fidelity image synthesis and editing [ 14 , 30 , 26 ] , motivating diffusion-based style transfer methods based on inversion, attention manipulation, reference feature injection, or training-free guidance [ 37 , 19 , 6 , 33 ] . Despite this progress, training-free diffusion style transfer still faces a difficult trade-off among style fidelity, content preservation, and content leakage suppression. A style reference image is not a pure style signal: it often contains colors, textures, object identity, semantic content, and spatial layout. Directly injecting such features may therefore transfer undesired content from the style reference to the generated image, a problem observed in recent reference-guided stylization and personalization methods [ 33 , 27 ] . In addition, strong attention replacement or feature injection can improve stylization but may overwrite the original content trajectory and distort object structure [ 6 ] . Finally, most guidance strategies still rely on fixed or heuristic schedules [ 15 , 2 , 35 , 34 ] , despite the time-dependent and state-dependent nature of diffusion sampling. Recent uncertainty-aware diffusion studies show that uncertainty can identify unreliable denoising regions by estimating generation confidence or score variance under perturbations [ 18 , 7 ] . This motivates using uncertainty as a state-dependent signal to adapt guidance along the reverse trajectory. Motivated by these observations, we propose TRACE , a training-free framework for diffusion-based style transfer. TRACE treats stylization as a controlled denoising process instead of a static feature-transfer operation. First, TRACE performs an offline CLIP-based content-style subspace decomposition from paired content-style data. At inference time, the learned subspaces remove content-related components from the style reference and style-related components from the content reference, reducing reference-induced leakage before sampling. Second, TRACE introduces residual attention control, which injects the cleaned style signal as an additive residual rather than directly replacing attention features. This preserves the content trajectory while allowing style cues to interact with content geometry. Third, TRACE formulates style guidance as a time-dependent control signal and adapts it according to the uncertainty of the current denoising state, strengthening corrective guidance in unstable states while avoiding excessive perturbation in stable ones. Our contributions are summarized as follows: • We propose a CLIP-based content-style decomposition mechanism that reduces reference-induced content leakage before diffusion sampling. • A residual style injection is introduced to control the injection of style information additively without directly overwriting the content generation trajectory. • We also formulate training-free diffusion style transfer as a time-dependent control problem and develop an uncertainty-aware adaptive guidance strategy for state-dependent stylization control. • Extensive quantitative, qualitative, and ablation studies show that TRACE achieves a favorable balance among style fidelity, content preservation, and leakage suppression.

sections.heading: 2.1 Training-free Diffusion Style Transfer
sections.text: Diffusion models have become powerful generative priors for image synthesis and editing through iterative denoising [ 14 , 30 , 31 ] , while Latent Diffusion Models improve efficiency by operating in a compressed latent space with flexible attention-based conditioning [ 26 ] . These advances have motivated diffusion-based style transfer methods that exploit pretrained diffusion models. InST [ 37 ] learns a style representation from a single painting through inversion, and DiffuseIT [ 19 ] performs image-guided translation with disentangled content and style representations. More recent training-free methods avoid fine-tuning by manipulating attention or reference features. StyleID [ 6 ] injects style information through self-attention feature manipulation, while InstantStyle [ 33 ] emphasizes the need to decouple style and content information in feature space. Despite their effectiveness, training-free reference-guided methods still face a difficult trade-off between stylization strength and content preservation. A style image often contains not only colors, textures, and artistic patterns, but also object identity, spatial layout, and scene semantics. Directly injecting such entangled features may cause content leakage, where undesired semantic structures from the style reference appear in the output [ 33 , 27 ] . Existing methods reduce this issue through feature statistics, attention matching, or feature decoupling [ 17 , 22 , 19 , 33 , 16 ] . However, most training-free methods do not explicitly remove content-related components from the style reference before sampling. TRACE addresses this limitation by learning CLIP-based content and style subspaces, which are used to clean both references before attention-based style injection.

sections.heading: 2.2 Attention Control and Adaptive Guidance
sections.text: Attention layers provide an effective interface for controlling diffusion generation. Prompt-to-Prompt [ 12 ] shows that cross-attention maps are closely related to spatial layout, and subsequent works exploit attention features for editing, personalization, and style transfer [ 21 , 32 , 6 ] . However, direct attention replacement or key-value injection can overwrite the content trajectory, especially when the style reference contains strong semantic structures. This motivates residual attention control, where style information is injected additively while preserving the original content generation path. Guidance is another important mechanism for steering diffusion sampling. Classifier-free guidance [ 15 ] modifies the denoising trajectory to improve condition adherence, while training-free guidance methods use external objectives or energy functions without updating model weights [ 2 , 35 , 5 , 34 ] . However, most guidance strategies rely on fixed scales or heuristic schedules, which do not fully account for the time-dependent and state-dependent nature of reverse diffusion. Recent works interpret diffusion sampling as trajectory optimization or stochastic optimal control [ 27 , 1 ] , suggesting that guidance should be treated as a dynamic control signal. Motivated by this view, TRACE introduces uncertainty-aware time-dependent guidance that adapts the control strength according to the stability of each denoising state.

The estimated clean latent x ^ 0 | t \hat{x}_{0|t} serves as an intermediate prediction of the final sample and provides a convenient representation for computing style objectives and guiding the denoising trajectory.

sections.heading: 4 Methodology
sections.text: Figure 1 : Overview of our approach ( TRACE ). TRACE first learns content and style subspaces from paired CLIP embeddings in an offline stage. During inference, it cleans the content and style representations through subspace projection, injects the cleaned style signal via residual style injection, and applies uncertainty-aware time-dependent guidance to control the reverse diffusion trajectory. A detailed TRACE sampling algorithm is provided in Appendix 0.B.2 .

sections.heading: 4.1 Overview
sections.text: Given a content image I c I_{c} and a style reference I s I_{s} , TRACE generates a stylized image I c ​ s I_{cs} in a training-free manner by reusing a pretrained diffusion model (StableCascade [ 23 ] ) without updating its parameters. TRACE first performs an offline CLIP-based content-style decomposition, where paired content-style embeddings are used to estimate a content subspace Q content Q_{\mathrm{content}} and a style subspace Q style Q_{\mathrm{style}} via Singular Value Decomposition (SVD) [ 11 ] . During inference, these subspaces are used to remove style-related components from the content representation and content-related components from the style representation, yielding cleaned embeddings that reduce reference-induced leakage. The cleaned style signal is then injected through residual attention, preserving the content generation trajectory while transferring style information. Finally, TRACE applies uncertainty-aware adaptive guidance at each denoising step, where the style guidance direction g t g_{t} is modulated by the denoising uncertainty Σ t \Sigma_{t} to provide stronger correction in unstable states and more conservative updates in reliable states.

sections.heading: 4.3 Residual Style Injection
sections.text: After content-style cleaning, TRACE injects the cleaned style signal into the diffusion model by making use of cross-attention. Let z [ base , content ] t z^{t}_{[\text{base},\text{content}]} denote the latent feature at timestep t t obtained by cross-attention using the base query and K, V constructed from the self-attention feature and the content representation. This branch mainly preserves the spatial structure of the current diffusion trajectory while injecting content information into the latent representation. To extract the stylization effect, TRACE compares two cleaned attention outputs: z [ style , content ] clean z^{\text{clean}}_{[\text{style},\text{content}]} , obtained by jointly using the cleaned style and content representations, and z content clean z^{\text{clean}}_{\text{content}} , obtained from the cleaned content representation alone. Their difference gives a residual style signal: Δ ​ z clean = z [ style , content ] clean − z content clean . \Delta z^{\text{clean}}=z^{\text{clean}}_{[\text{style},\text{content}]}-z^{\text{clean}}_{\text{content}}. (20) This residual captures the style information that is injected when the style representation interacts with the content structure. Using both content and style in the attention computation is important because injecting style alone may break the spatial layout or object structure, while the joint content-style attention keeps the stylization aligned with the content geometry. The final latent feature is updated as z t = z [ base , content ] t + λ t ​ Δ ​ z clean , z^{t}=z^{t}_{[\text{base},\text{content}]}+\lambda_{t}\Delta z^{\text{clean}}, (21) where λ t \lambda_{t} controls the strength of residual style injection. As a result, TRACE can inject visible style information while still preserving the spatial structure and semantic content of the input image.

sections.heading: 5.1 Baselines
sections.text: TRACE is compared with two groups of representative training-free diffusion baselines. Stylization methods, including StyleID [ 6 ] , AttenST [ 16 ] , DiffuseIT [ 19 ] , and InstantStyle [ 33 ] , mainly focus on transferring visual style through feature, attention, or reference-guided manipulation. OC-based methods, including RB-Modulation [ 27 ] and ITOC [ 4 ] , emphasize controlled reverse diffusion and source preservation. Detailed descriptions of all methods and implementation settings of TRACE are provided in Appendix 0.D.1 and 0.D.2 , respectively.

sections.heading: 5.2 Dataset
sections.text: For inference-time style transfer evaluation, we use 15 style reference images from the StyleAligned benchmark [ 13 ] and 13 content images from DreamBooth [ 28 ] . For the offline content-style decomposition stage, we use the paired content-style data from RB-Modulation [ 27 ] . Detailed statistics and analysis of the decomposition dataset are provided in Appendix 0.C.1 .

sections.heading: 5.3 Evaluation Metrics
sections.text: We evaluate TRACE from three aspects: style fidelity , content preservation , and content leakage . • Style fidelity is measured by CSD style similarity (CSD) [ 29 ] and Style Retrieval Accuracy (SRA). • Content preservation is measured by CLIP image similarity (CLIP-I) [ 25 ] , DINO image similarity (DINO) [ 3 ] , and Learned Perceptual Image Patch Similarity (LPIPS) [ 36 ] . • Content leakage is measured by Directional Content Leakage (DCL). Detailed metric definitions are provided in Appendix 0.D.3 .

sections.heading: 6 Results
sections.text: The parameters for main experiment are selected based on Sec. 7 , while the subspace rank analysis is provided in Appendix 0.C.2 .

sections.heading: 6.1 Qualitative Results
sections.text: Figure 2 : Qualitative comparison with training-free style transfer methods. Red, purple, and cyan boxes denote TRACE, OC-based methods, and stylization methods, respectively. More visualizations are provided in Appendix 0.E.4 . Figure 2 shows qualitative comparisons between TRACE and existing training-free baselines. OC-based methods such as ITOC and RB-Modulation generally preserve the content structure and produce visually stable images, but their stylization strength is relatively weak, especially when the target style requires more than simple color transfer. In contrast, stylization-oriented methods such as AttenST, StyleID, InstantStyle, and DiffuseIT often produce stronger style effects, but they may distort the object structure or introduce semantic content from the style reference. This is mainly because strong attention manipulation or AdaIN can act as a direct information transfer between the content and style images, which improves style fidelity but also increases the risk of content leakage. TRACE achieves a more balanced result. It preserves the main object layout and spatial structure while injecting visible style patterns into the generated image. The advantage is particularly clear for styles that involve structural changes (samples 3, 4) rather than only color shifts (samples 1, 2). These results demonstrate that the proposed content-style decomposition, residual style injection, and uncertainty-time adaptive guidance jointly improve stylization quality without severely damaging the content structure. Additional qualitative comparisons and diverse stylization results are provided in Appendix 0.E.8 .

sections.heading: Comparison with Stylization Methods:
sections.text: Table 1 compares TRACE with representative diffusion-based stylization methods. StyleID and AttenST achieve the highest style scores in terms of CSD and SRA, showing that strong attention-based stylization can effectively transfer visual appearance. However, these methods provide weaker content preservation than TRACE, as reflected by lower DINO and CLIP-I scores. DiffuseIT and InstantStyle also show noticeable degradation in content consistency, especially on DINO, CLIP-I, and LPIPS. In contrast, TRACE achieves the best content preservation on DINO and CLIP-I, while maintaining competitive style fidelity. Although TRACE does not obtain the highest style scores, it significantly reduces semantic leakage from the style reference, achieving the lowest DCL among all compared stylization methods. This indicates that TRACE better preserves the semantic structure of the content image while avoiding undesired transfer of object identity or layout from the style image.

sections.heading: Comparison with OC-based Methods:
sections.text: Table 1 compares our approach with optimal-control-based methods, including RB-Modulation and ITOC. These methods achieve strong content preservation, as shown by higher DINO and CLIP-I scores and lower LPIPS and DCL values. This indicates that OC-based methods are effective at maintaining the source structure and reducing semantic leakage from the style reference. However, their stylization strength is limited, with substantially lower CSD and SRA scores than TRACE. In contrast, TRACE significantly improves style fidelity over both RB-Modulation and ITOC, achieving the best CSD and SRA scores among this group. Although TRACE has slightly weaker content-preservation and leakage scores than these conservative OC-based baselines, it provides much stronger stylization while still maintaining reasonable content consistency. These results show that TRACE provides a better style-content trade-off for reference-guided style transfer.

sections.heading: 7.1 Effect of Content-Style Decomposition
sections.text: We first analyze the effect of content-style decomposition by comparing E0 with E1 and E2 in Tab. 2 . Without decomposition, E1 achieves the highest style scores, but its content preservation drops significantly and its DCL becomes much higher. This indicates that directly using the style reference can transfer strong visual appearance, but it also introduces semantic leakage from the style image. In contrast, full decomposition in E2 improves content preservation and reduces leakage, but it also removes useful style information, leading to weaker stylization. The soft decomposition used in TRACE provides a better balance between these two extremes, maintaining effective style transfer while reducing content leakage.

sections.heading: 7.2 Effect of Residual Style Injection
sections.text: We then evaluate the effect of residual style injection by comparing E0 with E3. The original cross-attention variant in E3 preserves content well, as shown by higher DINO and CLIP-I scores and lower leakage. However, its style fidelity is much weaker, suggesting that the style signal is insufficiently injected into the denoising trajectory. By contrast, the residual style injection in TRACE substantially improves CSD and SRA while still keeping reasonable content preservation. This confirms that adding a content-aligned stylization residual is more effective than conservative attention fusion for reference-guided style transfer. The detail of original cross-attention is provided in Appendix 0.E.1 .

sections.heading: 7.3 Effect of Time-adaptive Guidance
sections.text: To study the effect of guidance strength, we compare E0 with E4-E6. From no adaptive guidance in E4 to constant guidance with λ = 1 \lambda=1 in E5, stronger guidance improves stylization, indicating that an appropriate control signal is necessary for transferring style effectively. However, further increasing the fixed guidance scale to λ = 2 \lambda=2 in E6 leads to overly aggressive stylization, which weakens content preservation and increases leakage. This trend shows that a fixed guidance value is difficult to balance across different denoising states. In contrast, TRACE uses uncertainty-time adaptive guidance to adjust the control strength along the reverse trajectory, achieving a better balance between style fidelity and content preservation. Additional analyses of timestep-wise uncertainty and adaptive guidance are provided in Appendices 0.E.2 and 0.E.5 .

sections.heading: 7.4 Effect of Noise-level Scheduling
sections.text: To study the effect of the starting noise level, we compare different values of ρ \rho . Instead of starting from pure noise, TRACE starts sampling from a fixed intermediate noising step, which helps preserve the pose and spatial structure of the content image. When ρ = 1.0 \rho=1.0 , the trajectory starts from a highly noisy state, it allows stronger stylization but causes noticeable content distortion and leakage. When ρ = 0.5 \rho=0.5 , more content information is retained, leading to better pose preservation but weaker style transfer. We therefore use ρ = 0.7 \rho=0.7 in TRACE, which provides a better balance between preserving the content pose and enabling sufficient stylization. Additional visual results under different noise levels are provided in Appendix 0.E.3 .

sections.heading: 8 Conclusion
sections.text: In this paper, we presented TRACE, a training-free diffusion framework for reference-guided style transfer. TRACE integrates content-style decomposition, residual style injection, and uncertainty-time adaptive guidance to balance style fidelity, content preservation, and leakage suppression. Experiments show that TRACE better preserves content structure and reduces semantic leakage compared with stylization methods while achieving stronger stylization than OC-based baselines. However, TRACE still has limitations when the style reference contains strong structural patterns or shape-dominant elements. In such cases, the transferred style may affect the pose, contour, or fine geometry of the content object, leading to imperfect shape preservation. In future work, we will explore more explicit structure- and pose-preserving mechanisms to further protect the spatial layout of the content image during style injection.

sections.text: This section derives the uncertainty-aware guidance update used in TRACE. We first formulate diffusion guidance as an uncertainty-shaped stochastic optimal control problem, derive the corresponding global optimality condition, and then obtain a tractable local controller used in our sampling procedure.

Since style objectives are naturally evaluated on clean latent estimates, TRACE applies the control directly to x ^ 0 | t \hat{x}_{0|t} . The timestep guidance direction is defined as g t = ∇ x ^ 0 | t ℒ s ​ ( x ^ 0 | t , I s ) . g_{t}=\nabla_{\hat{x}_{0|t}}\mathcal{L}_{\mathrm{s}}\left(\hat{x}_{0|t};I_{s}\right). (41) For a small local perturbation u t u_{t} , we approximate the style objective by first-order Taylor expansion: ℒ s ​ ( x ^ 0 | t + u t , I s ) ≈ ℒ s ​ ( x ^ 0 | t , I s ) + g t ⊤ ​ u t . \mathcal{L}_{\mathrm{s}}\left(\hat{x}_{0|t}+u_{t};I_{s}\right)\approx\mathcal{L}_{\mathrm{s}}\left(\hat{x}_{0|t};I_{s}\right)+g_{t}^{\top}u_{t}. (42) Since the first term is constant with respect to u t u_{t} , the local one-step control problem becomes min u t 1 2 ​ u t ⊤ ​ Σ t − 1 ​ u t + g t ⊤ ​ u t . \min_{u_{t}}\quad\frac{1}{2}u_{t}^{\top}\Sigma_{t}^{-1}u_{t}+g_{t}^{\top}u_{t}. (43) Because Σ t ≻ 0 \Sigma_{t}\succ 0 , the objective in Eq. 43 is strictly convex and has a unique minimizer. Taking the derivative with respect to u t u_{t} gives ∇ u t ( 1 2 ​ u t ⊤ ​ Σ t − 1 ​ u t + g t ⊤ ​ u t ) = Σ t − 1 ​ u t + g t . \nabla_{u_{t}}\left(\frac{1}{2}u_{t}^{\top}\Sigma_{t}^{-1}u_{t}+g_{t}^{\top}u_{t}\right)=\Sigma_{t}^{-1}u_{t}+g_{t}. (44) Setting the derivative to zero yields Σ t − 1 ​ u t ⋆ + g t = 0 . \Sigma_{t}^{-1}u_{t}^{\star}+g_{t}=0. (45) Thus, Σ t − 1 ​ u t ⋆ = − g t . \Sigma_{t}^{-1}u_{t}^{\star}=-g_{t}. (46) Multiplying both sides by Σ t \Sigma_{t} , we obtain the closed-form local control: u t ⋆ = − Σ t ​ g t . u_{t}^{\star}=-\Sigma_{t}g_{t}. (47) This local controller can be viewed as a tractable one-step approximation of the global uncertainty-shaped control in Eq. 40 . The adjoint direction in the global solution is replaced by the instantaneous style gradient g t g_{t} , while the uncertainty-shaped gain Σ t \Sigma_{t} is retained to modulate the control strength.

sections.heading: 0.A.3 TRACE Guidance Update
sections.text: TRACE applies the closed-form local control in Eq. 47 to the predicted clean latent: x ~ 0 | t = x ^ 0 | t + u t ⋆ = x ^ 0 | t − Σ t ​ g t . \widetilde{x}_{0|t}=\hat{x}_{0|t}+u_{t}^{\star}=\hat{x}_{0|t}-\Sigma_{t}g_{t}. (48) The updated clean estimate x ~ 0 | t \widetilde{x}_{0|t} is then used in the DDIM transition: x t − 1 = DDIM ⁡ ( x ~ 0 | t , x t ) . x_{t-1}=\mathrm{DDIM}\left(\widetilde{x}_{0|t},x_{t}\right). (49) Therefore, the TRACE update is a local uncertainty-shaped control step applied during reverse diffusion. When the denoising state is uncertain, Σ t \Sigma_{t} increases the effective guidance strength and allows stronger corrective updates. When the state is reliable, the update remains more conservative, helping preserve the content trajectory.

sections.heading: 0.C.1 Construction of Paired Content-Style Dataset
sections.text: Figure 4 : Representative paired content-style samples used for decomposition analysis. Rows show content identities and columns show style references. To estimate the offline content and style subspaces, we construct a paired content-style dataset from 350 content images and 100 style images. Instead of exhaustively combining all content and style references, we randomly sample 10 style images for each content image, producing 3,500 stylized pairs in total. Each generated pair is associated with a content index and a style index, allowing us to analyze content-specific and style-specific variations in the CLIP embedding space. We split the 3,500 paired samples into 3,150 pairs for offline subspace estimation and 350 held-out pairs for decomposition analysis and validation. sections.heading: 0.D.1 Baseline Details
sections.text: We compare TRACE with two groups of diffusion-based baselines: Stylization methods and OC-based methods.

sections.heading: Stylization methods:
sections.text: This group focuses on transferring visual appearance from a style reference. StyleID [ 6 ] transfers style by manipulating diffusion features and attention representations between the content and style images. AttenST [ 16 ] injects style information through attention-based manipulation. DiffuseIT [ 19 ] performs diffusion-based image translation and stylization using iterative guidance. InstantStyle [ 33 ] uses reference-guided style injection to transfer style information while reducing content interference.

sections.heading: OC-based methods:
sections.text: This group focuses on controlling the reverse diffusion trajectory. RB-Modulation [ 27 ] modulates the reverse sampling process to preserve the source image while steering generation toward the target condition. ITOC [ 4 ] formulates diffusion sampling as a trajectory optimization problem and controls the reverse process during inference.

sections.heading: Style Retrieval Accuracy (SRA).
sections.text: SRA evaluates whether the generated image can be correctly retrieved as the target style from a style reference gallery. For each generated image I c ​ s i I_{cs}^{i} , we extract its CSD style embedding and compare it with the CSD embeddings of all style reference images using cosine similarity. The retrieved style is defined as the nearest style reference in the gallery. SRA is computed as: SRA = 1 N ∑ i = 1 N 𝟏 [ arg max j cos ( ϕ CSD ( I c ​ s i ) , ϕ CSD ( I s j ) ) = y s i ] , \mathrm{SRA}=\frac{1}{N}\sum_{i=1}^{N}\mathbf{1}\left[\arg\max_{j}\cos\left(\phi_{\mathrm{CSD}}(I_{cs}^{i}),\phi_{\mathrm{CSD}}(I_{s}^{j})\right)=y_{s}^{i}\right], (50) where ϕ CSD \phi_{\mathrm{CSD}} denotes the CSD style encoder, I s j I_{s}^{j} denotes a style reference image in the gallery, and y s i y_{s}^{i} is the target style label of the i i -th generated image. A higher SRA indicates that the generated image is more recognizable as the target style.

sections.heading: Directional Content Leakage (DCL).
sections.text: DCL evaluates whether the generated image moves toward the semantic structure of the style reference. We compute DCL in a content/structure feature space using DINO features extracted from grayscale images, which reduces the influence of color and low-level style statistics. Let f c f_{c} , f s f_{s} , and f g f_{g} denote the normalized DINO features of the content image, style image, and generated image, respectively. DCL is defined as: DCL = clip [ 0 , 1 ] ⁡ ( ( f g − f c ) ⊤ ​ ( f s − f c ) ‖ f s − f c ‖ 2 2 + ϵ ) . \mathrm{DCL}=\operatorname{clip}_{[0,1]}\left(\frac{(f_{g}-f_{c})^{\top}(f_{s}-f_{c})}{\|f_{s}-f_{c}\|_{2}^{2}+\epsilon}\right). (51) A larger DCL indicates that the generated image moves more strongly from the content image toward the style reference in the structure feature space, suggesting stronger content leakage. Therefore, lower DCL is better.

sections.heading: 0.E.1 Residual Style Injection vs. Original Attention
sections.text: (a) Residual style injection (b) Original attention Figure 5 : Comparison between residual style injection and original attention. As shown in Fig. 5 , the original attention strategy combines multiple attention outputs by simple averaging. Specifically, the outputs obtained from base-content attention, style-content attention, and content-only attention are averaged to produce the final representation. Although this strategy mixes style and content information, it treats all branches equally and may dilute the style signal or disturb the content trajectory. In contrast, the residual style injection used in TRACE keeps the base-content attention output as the main trajectory and injects style only through an additive residual. The residual is computed by subtracting the content-only attention output from the style-content attention output and then adding the scaled difference to the base-content representation. This way allows us to preserve the original content trajectory while injecting only the style-related residual information.

sections.heading: 0.E.2 Timestep-wise Uncertainty Analysis
sections.text: Figure 6 visualizes the estimated uncertainty maps across denoising steps. At early timesteps, the predicted clean preview x ~ 0 | t \widetilde{x}_{0|t} is still ambiguous, and the uncertainty is high and spatially diffuse. As denoising progresses, the object structure becomes clearer and the uncertainty gradually decreases. In particular, the regions corresponding to the main object, where the style has been injected, become more stable in the later timesteps. This can be observed from the uncertainty maps becoming less noisy and more concentrated, while the predicted clean previews show a more consistent object shape and appearance. These results indicate that uncertainty provides a useful reliability signal for adaptive guidance: stronger intervention is applied when the generation is unstable, while weaker intervention is used once the stylized object becomes stable. In contrast, very late steps already contain a stable content structure, which helps preserve the original image but leaves limited room for injecting the target style. sections.text: We first evaluate whether the proposed content-style decomposition can suppress semantic information carried by the style reference. As shown in Tab. 8 , removing the decomposition substantially degrades content preservation and increases semantic leakage. This indicates that the decomposition reduces reference-induced semantic leakage while preserving the desired visual style. sections.heading: Held-out style-family generalization.
sections.text: We further examine whether the learned content-style subspaces generalize beyond the style families used during offline decomposition. For this evaluation, the target style family is excluded from the offline subspace construction and used only at inference time. As shown in Tab. 8 , performance remains nearly unchanged when the target style family is held out: CSD changes from 43.213 43.213 to 43.292 43.292 , DINO from 68.909 68.909 to 69.552 69.552 , and DCL from 19.333 19.333 to 19.162 19.162 . These results suggest that the learned subspaces capture reusable content and style directions rather than relying on the presence of the target style family during offline estimation. Figure 12 : Qualitative result on an unseen origami-style reference.

sections.heading: 0.E.7 Trade-off Analysis
sections.text: Style transfer involves competing objectives among style fidelity, content preservation, and semantic leakage. We therefore examine pairwise Pareto trade-offs among representative methods rather than relying on a single aggregate criterion. As shown in Fig. 13 , different methods occupy different regions of the trade-off space, highlighting the balance achieved by TRACE across the competing objectives. Figure 13 : Pairwise Pareto trade-offs among representative style-transfer methods.

sections.heading: Additional qualitative Comparison.
sections.text: Figure 14 and Fig. 15 provide additional qualitative comparisons under different style characteristics. For the texture-dominant style reference, baseline methods may transfer strong local patterns but can also introduce structural distortion or semantic leakage. For the color-dominant style reference, some baselines capture the global color distribution but may weaken content identity or object boundaries. In contrast, TRACE better preserves the main content structure while still transferring the target visual appearance, showing a more balanced style-content trade-off. To further illustrate the qualitative performance of TRACE, we provide additional stylization results on diverse content-style pairs in Fig. 16 .

sections.text: Our evaluation primarily uses StyleAligned and DreamBooth images, which are predominantly object-centric. Recent diffusion-based methods achieve impressive stylization quality by exploiting strong pretrained generative priors. However, training-free approaches still face a difficult trade-off among style fidelity, content preservation, and content leakage. Direct style injection may unintentionally transfer semantic content from the style image, while fixed guidance schedules often ignore the time- and state-dependent nature of diffusion sampling. To address these limitations, we propose TRACE , a training-free diffusion style transfer framework with T ime-adaptive R esidual A ttention Control and C ontent-Style d E composition. TRACE first performs offline CLIP-based subspace analysis to separate content and style directions from paired data. During inference, it removes content-related components from the style reference and style-related components from the content reference to reduce leakage. It then injects style information through residual cross-attention and applies uncertainty-aware guidance to adapt the guidance signal at each denoising step. Experiments show that TRACE achieves a favorable trade-off between stylization and preservation. Compared with optimal-control-based baselines, TRACE substantially improves style fidelity (+17.28 CSD and +34.10 SRA). While, compared with stylization methods, it better preserves content structure (+12.80 DINO, +5.52 CLIP-I, and -8.19 LPIPS) and reduces directional semantic leakage by 29.5% in DCL. Our code is publicly available at TRACE . Keywords: Style Transfer Content-Style Decomposition Time-Adaptive Guidance 1 Introduction Image style transfer aims to synthesize an image that preserves the semantic structure of a content image while adopting the visual appearance of a style reference. Early neural style transfer methods demonstrated that deep features can separate and recombine content and style representations [ 10 ] , while arbitrary style transfer methods improved efficiency through feature-statistics matching, whitening-and-coloring transforms, attention matching, and transformer-based fusion [ 17 , 20 , 22 , 8 ] . More recently, diffusion models have provided strong generative priors for high-fidelity image synthesis and editing [ 14 , 30 , 26 ] , motivating diffusion-based style transfer methods based on inversion, attention manipulation, reference feature injection, or training-free guidance [ 37 , 19 , 6 , 33 ] . Despite this progress, training-free diffusion style transfer still faces a difficult trade-off among style fidelity, content preservation, and content leakage suppression. A style reference image is not a pure style signal: it often contains colors, textures, object identity, semantic content, and spatial layout. Directly injecting such features may therefore transfer undesired content from the style reference to the generated image, a problem observed in recent reference-guided stylization and personalization methods [ 33 , 27 ] . In addition, strong attention replacement or feature injection can improve stylization but may overwrite the original content trajectory and distort object structure [ 6 ] . Finally, most guidance strategies still rely on fixed or heuristic schedules [ 15 , 2 , 35 , 34 ] , despite the time-dependent and state-dependent nature of diffusion sampling. Recent uncertainty-aware diffusion studies show that uncertainty can identify unreliable denoising regions by estimating generation confidence or score variance under perturbations [ 18 , 7 ] . This motivates using uncertainty as a state-dependent signal to adapt guidance along the reverse trajectory. Motivated by these observations, we propose TRACE , a training-free framework for diffusion-based style transfer. TRACE treats stylization as a controlled denoising process instead of a static feature-transfer operation. First, TRACE performs an offline CLIP-based content-style subspace decomposition from paired content-style data. At inference time, the learned subspaces remove content-related components from the style reference and style-related components from the content reference, reducing reference-induced leakage before sampling. Second, TRACE introduces residual attention control, which injects the cleaned style signal as an additive residual rather than directly replacing attention features. This preserves the content trajectory while allowing style cues to interact with content geometry. Third, TRACE formulates style guidance as a time-dependent control signal and adapts it according to the uncertainty of the current denoising state, strengthening corrective guidance in unstable states while avoiding excessive perturbation in stable ones. Our contributions are summarized as follows: • We propose a CLIP-based content-style decomposition mechanism that reduces reference-induced content leakage before diffusion sampling. • A residual style injection is introduced to control the injection of style information additively without directly overwriting the content generation trajectory. • We also formulate training-free diffusion style transfer as a time-dependent control problem and develop an uncertainty-aware adaptive guidance strategy for state-dependent stylization control. • Extensive quantitative, qualitative, and ablation studies show that TRACE achieves a favorable balance among style fidelity, content preservation, and leakage suppression. 2 Related Work 2.1 Training-free Diffusion Style Transfer Diffusion models have become powerful generative priors for image synthesis and editing through iterative denoising [ 14 , 30 , 31 ] , while Latent Diffusion Models improve efficiency by operating in a compressed latent space with flexible attention-based conditioning [ 26 ] . These advances have motivated diffusion-based style transfer methods that exploit pretrained diffusion models. InST [ 37 ] learns a style representation from a single painting through inversion, and DiffuseIT [ 19 ] performs image-guided translation with disentangled content and style representations. More recent training-free methods avoid fine-tuning by manipulating attention or reference features. StyleID [ 6 ] injects style information through self-attention feature manipulation, while InstantStyle [ 33 ] emphasizes the need to decouple style and content information in feature space. Despite their effectiveness, training-free reference-guided methods still face a difficult trade-off between stylization strength and content preservation. A style image often contains not only colors, textures, and artistic patterns, but also object identity, spatial layout, and scene semantics. Directly injecting such entangled features may cause content leakage, where undesired semantic structures from the style reference appear in the output [ 33 , 27 ] . Existing methods reduce this issue through feature statistics, attention matching, or feature decoupling [ 17 , 22 , 19 , 33 , 16 ] . However, most training-free methods do not explicitly remove content-related components from the style reference before sampling. TRACE addresses this limitation by learning CLIP-based content and style subspaces, which are used to clean both references before attention-based style injection. 2.2 Attention Control and Adaptive Guidance Attention layers provide an effective interface for controlling diffusion generation. Prompt-to-Prompt [ 12 ] shows that cross-attention maps are closely related to spatial layout, and subsequent works exploit attention features for editing, personalization, and style transfer [ 21 , 32 , 6 ] . However, direct attention replacement or key-value injection can overwrite the content trajectory, especially when the style reference contains strong semantic structures. This motivates residual attention control, where style information is injected additively while preserving the original content generation path. Guidance is another important mechanism for steering diffusion sampling. Classifier-free guidance [ 15 ] modifies the denoising trajectory to improve condition adherence, while training-free guidance methods use external objectives or energy functions without updating model weights [ 2 , 35 , 5 , 34 ] . However, most guidance strategies rely on fixed scales or heuristic schedules, which do not fully account for the time-dependent and state-dependent nature of reverse diffusion. Recent works interpret diffusion sampling as trajectory optimization or stochastic optimal control [ 27 , 1 ] , suggesting that guidance should be treated as a dynamic control signal. Motivated by this view, TRACE introduces uncertainty-aware time-dependent guidance that adapts the control strength according to the stability of each denoising state. 3 Preliminaries 3.1 Diffusion Sampling Diffusion models generate samples by iteratively reversing a noising process. However, many guidance objectives are naturally defined on clean images rather than noisy intermediate states. TRACE first learns content and style subspaces from paired CLIP embeddings in an offline stage. During inference, it cleans the content and style representations through subspace projection, injects the cleaned style signal via residual style injection, and applies uncertainty-aware time-dependent guidance to control the reverse diffusion trajectory. A detailed TRACE sampling algorithm is provided in Appendix 0.B.2 . 4.1 Overview Given a content image I c I_{c} and a style reference I s I_{s} , TRACE generates a stylized image I c ​ s I_{cs} in a training-free manner by reusing a pretrained diffusion model (StableCascade [ 23 ] ) without updating its parameters. During inference, these subspaces are used to remove style-related components from the content representation and content-related components from the style representation, yielding cleaned embeddings that reduce reference-induced leakage. The cleaned style signal is then injected through residual attention, preserving the content generation trajectory while transferring style information. Finally, TRACE applies uncertainty-aware adaptive guidance at each denoising step, where the style guidance direction g t g_{t} is modulated by the denoising uncertainty Σ t \Sigma_{t} to provide stronger correction in unstable states and more conservative updates in reliable states. 4.2 Offline Content-Style Decomposition A style reference image is usually not a pure style signal. Stylization methods, including StyleID [ 6 ] , AttenST [ 16 ] , DiffuseIT [ 19 ] , and InstantStyle [ 33 ] , mainly focus on transferring visual style through feature, attention, or reference-guided manipulation. OC-based methods, including RB-Modulation [ 27 ] and ITOC [ 4 ] , emphasize controlled reverse diffusion and source preservation. Detailed descriptions of all methods and implementation settings of TRACE are provided in Appendix 0.D.1 and 0.D.2 , respectively. 5.2 Dataset For inference-time style transfer evaluation, we use 15 style reference images from the StyleAligned benchmark [ 13 ] and 13 content images from DreamBooth [ 28 ] . For the offline content-style decomposition stage, we use the paired content-style data from RB-Modulation [ 27 ] . Detailed statistics and analysis of the decomposition dataset are provided in Appendix 0.C.1 . 5.3 Evaluation Metrics We evaluate TRACE from three aspects: style fidelity , content preservation , and content leakage . • Style fidelity is measured by CSD style similarity (CSD) [ 29 ] and Style Retrieval Accuracy (SRA). • Content preservation is measured by CLIP image similarity (CLIP-I) [ 25 ] , DINO image similarity (DINO) [ 3 ] , and Learned Perceptual Image Patch Similarity (LPIPS) [ 36 ] . • Content leakage is measured by Directional Content Leakage (DCL). This trend shows that a fixed guidance value is difficult to balance across different denoising states.
